questions.question: A Pareto type II loss X has survivor $\mathbb{P}(X>x)=[\beta/(\beta+x)]^\alpha$ for $x\ge0$, with shape $\alpha>0$ and scale $\beta>0$. What is the role of beta in the loss support?
options: It is the smallest possible loss; losses below beta are excluded.
It sets the loss scale; losses below beta are possible.
It is the largest possible loss; losses above beta are excluded.
It is the probability of zero loss; the rest are positive.

questions.question: A Pareto type II survivor is $[\beta/(\beta+x)]^\alpha$ for $x\ge0$, with scale $\beta>0$ and shape $\alpha=1/2$. Its mean is infinite. Does that make the probability law invalid?
options: Yes; a valid non-negative loss law must have finite mean.
Yes; the survivor must integrate to one to be a law.
No; it remains a valid law with an infinite mean.
No; infinite mean means every realised loss is infinite.

questions.question: A Pareto type II loss has scale $\beta>0$ and shape $\alpha=1$, so $\mathbb{P}(X>x)=\beta/(\beta+x)$ for $x\ge0$. What is the mean at this boundary shape?
options: It is infinite, because the survivor integral diverges.
It is zero, because the mean denominator alpha minus one is zero.
It equals beta, as for shape two.
It is negative, because the mean formula changes sign at one.

questions.question: A Pareto type II loss has scale $\beta>0$ and shape $\alpha=3/2$. Which moment statement is correct for this valid loss law?
options: Both mean and variance are finite because shape is positive.
Both mean and variance are infinite because shape is below two.
Its mean is infinite, but its variance is finite.
Its mean is finite, but its variance is infinite.

questions.question: A Pareto type II loss X has shape $\alpha>0$ and scale $\beta>0$, with survivor $[\beta/(\beta+x)]^\alpha$. The same losses are recorded as $Y=cX$ for constant $c>0$. Which parameter change gives the law of Y?
options: The shape becomes c alpha and the scale remains beta.
Both shape and scale are multiplied by c.
The shape remains alpha and the scale becomes c beta.
The shape remains alpha and the scale becomes beta divided by c.

questions.question: A Pareto type II loss has shape two, scale ten and survivor $[10/(10+x)]^2$ for $x\ge0$. What is $\mathbb{P}(X>10)$?
A Pareto type II loss has shape one, scale four and survivor $4/(4+x)$ for $x\ge0$. What median m satisfies $\mathbb{P}(X>m)=1/2$?
A Pareto type II loss has shape $\alpha=3$ and scale $\beta=2$. Its variance for shape above two is $\beta^2\alpha/[(\alpha-1)^2(\alpha-2)]$. What is the variance?
A Pareto type II ground-up loss has survivor $[2/(2+x)]^2$ for $x\ge0$. Under ordinary deductible two, per-loss payment is $Y=\max(X-2,0)$. What is $\mathbb{P}(Y=0)$?
Two Pareto type II losses have the same positive scale beta but shapes $0<\alpha_1<\alpha_2$. At a fixed threshold $x>0$, how do their exceedance probabilities compare?
options: $\mathbb{P}(X_1>x)<\mathbb{P}(X_2>x)$.
$\mathbb{P}(X_1>x)>\mathbb{P}(X_2>x)$.
$\mathbb{P}(X_1>x)=\mathbb{P}(X_2>x)$.
Their comparison cannot be made unless both variances are finite.

questions.question: A Pareto type II loss has shape $\alpha>0$, scale $\beta>0$ and survivor $[\beta/(\beta+x)]^\alpha$. Given $X>d$ for deductible $d>0$, which law describes the excess $X-d$?
options: Lomax with shape alpha and scale beta plus d.
Lomax with shape alpha and unchanged scale beta.
Lomax with shape alpha plus d and scale beta.
Lomax shifted to have its minimum at d.

questions.question: A Pareto type II loss has shape three and scale $\beta>0$, so its mean and variance are finite. For $t>0$, must $\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{e}^{tX}]$ also be finite?
options: No; every positive exponential moment of this model is infinite.
Yes; finite variance guarantees every positive exponential moment.
Yes; sufficiently small positive $t$ makes the exponential moment finite.
No; only for $t$ below $1/\beta$ is the exponential moment finite.

questions.question: A Pareto type II loss has shape two, scale four and ordinary deductible four. Its mean per-loss payment is $\mathbb{E}[(X-d)_+]=\beta^\alpha(\beta+d)^{1-\alpha}/(\alpha-1)$. What is that mean?
A Pareto type II loss has shape three and scale six. Given that it exceeds ordinary deductible four, its excess is Lomax with shape three and scale ten. What is the mean of a positive payment?

Loss A is Lomax with shape two and scale one; loss B has shape three and scale two. Both have mean one. Using their survivor formulas, which comparison at thresholds $1/2$ and ten shows that the common mean does not determine the tail?
options: $\mathbb{P}(A>1/2)=\mathbb{P}(B>1/2)$ and $\mathbb{P}(A>10)=\mathbb{P}(B>10)$.
$\mathbb{P}(A>1/2)<\mathbb{P}(B>1/2)$ but $\mathbb{P}(A>10)>\mathbb{P}(B>10)$.
$\mathbb{P}(A>1/2)>\mathbb{P}(B>1/2)$ and $\mathbb{P}(A>10)>\mathbb{P}(B>10)$.
$\mathbb{P}(A>1/2)<\mathbb{P}(B>1/2)$ and $\mathbb{P}(A>10)<\mathbb{P}(B>10)$.

questions.question: A Pareto type II loss has survivor $[\beta/(\beta+x)]^\alpha$ with $\alpha>0$, $\beta>0$. Let $R(x)=\mathbb{P}(X>2x\mid X>x)=[(\beta+x)/(\beta+2x)]^\alpha$. What is $\lim_{x\to\infty}R(x)$?
options: $0$, because every survivor tends to zero.
$1$, because conditioning removes the threshold.
$2^{-\alpha}$, a positive constant below one.
$2^{\alpha}$, because the larger threshold adds tail weight.
